Aftermarket hoses are sold for the examples, but no page loaded both said the part was new and named the example vehicle and year with a price (the one aftermarket page for the example truck does not say new). (2) A top labor time for the economy, midsize and luxury examples: the only stated times that qualify as range ends are a general guide's figure for one hose and a parts seller's time for the Ram 1500. No maker-stated time with a unit for replacing only a radiator hose on a passenger vehicle was found; the maker figures found include an inspection, cover a different hose or are for a heavy truck, so they are cross-checks.
unit: per job: one radiator hose, upper or lower, fitted with its clamps, with the coolant topped up or the drained amount replaced. Low = a quality aftermarket hose, high = the genuine hose at list (MSRP). Not included: the second hose, the thermostat, a full coolant flush, heater hoses, bypass or overflow hoses, the radiator, and diagnosis of a leak or of overheating

finding: Held: this file is not ready to publish. There is no live range for this job on the site today (live is null), so there is nothing to call too wide or too narrow; this is a first build. What was verified: the genuine hose at list is cheap on every example, $39.74 for the 2015 Toyota Corolla, $49.80 for the 2015 Honda CR-V, $107.00 for the 2015 Ram 1500 5.7L and $154.45 for the 2015 BMW 328i, each the dearest upper or lower radiator hose in the maker's dealer catalog. The only total that can be built at both ends of the labor range is the top for the truck: $107.00 + 2 hours x $160 = about $427 (the rate used for these checks is the national middle, $120-$160 an hour). Labor alone at the stated times is $60-$80 for half an hour and $240-$320 for two hours, so labor, not the hose, is most of this job, and the coolant is extra. What is null and why: (1) the low parts price for all four classes. Aftermarket hoses are sold for these vehicles, and one was seen for the Ram at $32.99, but no page loaded both said the part was new and named the example vehicle and year with a price, so no low is given and each class except the truck has only one parts source. (2) The top labor time for the economy, midsize and luxury examples. How solid the labor times are: weak. The low end everywhere is a general guide's statement that one hose usually takes less than 30 minutes, written for an owner and not for any vehicle. The truck's top is a parts seller's 2-hour installation time for an upper hose on the example truck, also written for an owner; the same seller says 1 hour for an older Ram. No maker-stated time with a unit for replacing only a radiator hose on a car or light truck was found. The maker figures that were found are cross-checks only: FCA's 1.0 hour to inspect and replace the lower radiator hose on a diesel Jeep Compass, FCA's 0.7 hour to inspect and replace a different coolant hose on a Dodge Durango 6.4L (both include an inspection, and both include draining and refilling the coolant), and Volvo Trucks' 0.6 hour for the upper radiator hose on a highway tractor. Taken together they point to roughly 0.6 to 1.0 hour as a warranty time when the coolant is drained and refilled, which would put a one-hose job at very roughly $110-$270 with a genuine hose, before coolant; that is a reading of cross-checks, not a sourced range, and it is not entered in the classes. A GM bulletin for the 2023-2026 Colorado and Canyon names a labor operation for radiator inlet hose replacement but prints no time. Benchmarks: Jerry $350-$630 (two hoses, 1 to 2.5 hours), RepairPal $304-$361 for the older Dodge Ram 1500 and $512-$547 for the later Ram 1500, YourMechanic about $251 on average. All three sit above what the cross-checks suggest for one hose, which fits their covering both hoses, more coolant or longer labor times; none says exactly what is included. Confidence is low: no class has a low parts price, three classes have one parts source, and only one labor figure is for an example vehicle. This is an estimate, not a quote and not a diagnosis.
extras: A quote often adds coolant (a top-up or a full drain and refill), new clamps if they are not supplied with the hose, bleeding air from the cooling system, a cooling system pressure test, shop supplies and sales tax. Shops often recommend replacing the other radiator hose at the same time, and sometimes the thermostat, the radiator cap or a coolant flush; each is priced separately from this estimate. On vehicles with quick-connect hose fittings the hose comes as an assembly with its connectors and costs more than a plain hose. If the hose was replaced because of a leak or overheating, finding the cause is a separate diagnosis charge. A hose replaced under a recall, service campaign or warranty is done by the dealer at no charge, so check for open campaigns first.
